results.summary: This design generates an animated VGA squares pattern based on the VGA playground rings template. Two input pins control the animation speed and direction, and the outputs drive a standard Tiny VGA pinout. It is tested either through a testbench or by connecting a VGA monitor. The documentation is brief and does not describe the visual output in detail.

This project generates a stripe pattern on a VGA display, based on the VGA playground template. It is intended as a quick test of an advanced workshop guide, and the input pins can be used to change the pattern. A VGA Pmod is required to view the output. The documentation is thin and does not specify what the input pins control.

This is a maze exploration game rendered on a 128x64 SSD1306 OLED display over I2C, with the player navigating a 16x8 hardcoded maze from start to goal. The core game logic is a combinational circuit generated from DSLX and wrapped in Verilog holding 123 bits of state, with up to two walls breakable and audio feedback through a piezo speaker. It requires an OLED, a piezo speaker, eight pushbuttons, and 4.7k pull-up resistors on the I2C lines. Buttons are synchronized and debounced, and the I2C runs at about 195 kHz using pseudo open-drain bidirectional pins.

This project implements a custom 8-bit RISC processor with a three-stage pipeline of fetch, decode, and execute. Program bytes are loaded through the input pins with a load mode and valid signal, and results are read from the output pins, with zero, carry, and negative flags exposed on the bidirectional pins. No external hardware is required, though a microcontroller or logic analyzer can be connected to automate program loading and capture results. The documentation is minimal and does not describe the instruction set or pipeline hazards.

This is a rudimentary implementation of the popular 2013 bird-flapping game, rendered over VGA. One input makes the bird go up and another starts the game, with output through a standard Tiny VGA pinout. A VGA Pmod is needed for video output, and a Python reference implementation is provided for comparison. The documentation notes that the reference and actual implementations have inputs offset by one cycle.

This project scrolls the text "hardened using python" across a 7-segment display. It is a demo for the microlane hardening flow and is intended to be run with a slow clock such as 5 Hz. No external hardware is required beyond the display itself. The documentation is brief and does not explain the microlane flow or the hardening results.

This design implements a 16-bit scrambler, framer, and error detector for safer transmissions, using gPEAC and Hammer18 circuits in a pipelined datapath. It supports bypass, encode, decode, and loopback modes selected by two control pins, with 18-bit words transmitted as two 9-bit half-words and an overall latency of five cycles. The design is intended for chaining multiple chips together, and custom boards or adapters are planned for verification. Decoding errors and zero flags are signalled but not acted upon, and the documentation notes several usage constraints such as not changing mode while data is in the pipeline.

This is a test, calibration, and design exploration design for the Wedgetail project, part of a PhD thesis. It contains a configurable array of ring oscillators, a digital phase-locked loop, and an SPI register file generated with SystemRDL, with the intent of verifying these components on real silicon. No external hardware is required, and the design also explores a logo-stamping workflow. The documentation is fairly detailed about the components but does not report silicon results.

This project is a VGA test design with a standard Tiny VGA pinout, but the documentation is essentially empty. The how-it-works, how-to-test, and external-hardware sections all say only "tbd". No functionality can be determined beyond the VGA output pins, and no external hardware is specified. The design cannot be meaningfully described from the available information.

This design plays a looping MOSS GIF animation and a "wiwiwi" sound, with the sprite and audio data stored in LUT-based ROMs. The sprite ROM holds four 64x64 frames scaled 4x and centered on a 640x480 VGA display, while the audio ROM holds 1-bit samples played back as 1-bit PCM on a bidirectional pin. It requires a TinyVGA Pmod and an Audio Pmod, and pulling an input pin high mutes the audio. The documentation is reasonably detailed about the data and display but does not describe the background animation in depth.
